title: The Benefits of Daylight through Windows

findings.antecedent: Daylight (as electromagnetic radiation)
findings.quote: Physically, daylight is just another source of electromagnetic radiation in the visible range. Electric light sources can be constructed to closely match a spectrum of daylight, but none have been made that mimic the variation in light spectrum that occurs with daylight at different times, in different seasons, and under different weather conditions.

findings.antecedent: Daylight
findings.consequent: Human visual system and circadian system stimulation
findings.quote: Physiologically, daylight is an effective stimulant to the human visual system and the human circadian system.

findings.antecedent: Daylight and a view
findings.quote: Psychologically, daylight and a view are much desired.

findings.antecedent: Daylight (delivered in large amounts with good spectrum)
findings.quote: Daylight does have a greater probability of maximizing visual performance than most forms of electric lighting because it tends to be delivered in large amounts with a spectrum that ensures excellent color rendering.

findings.antecedent: Daylight (poorly delivered, causing glare, distraction, veiling reflections, shadows)
findings.consequent: Visual discomfort, task difficulty, visual performance
findings.quote: Daylight can cause visual discomfort through glare and distraction, and it can diminish the stimuli the task presents to the visual system by producing veiling reflections or by shadows. The effectiveness of daylight for visual performance will depend on how it is delivered. The same conclusion applies to electric lighting. People will take action to reduce or eliminate daylight if it causes discomfort or increases task difficulty.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to bright light during the day and little or no light at night (daylighting)
findings.consequent: Entrainment of circadian system, performance of visual/non-visual tasks, long-term health problems
findings.quote: Exposure to bright light during the day and little or no light at night will accurately entrain the circadian system. Daylighting is an attractive way to deliver bright light during the day.

findings.antecedent: Windows (daylight and view)
findings.quote: Windows are strongly favored in work places for the daylight they deliver and the view out they provide, as long as they do not cause visual or thermal discomfort or a loss of privacy. Whether windows will produce an improvement in mood seems to depend on what the individual's preferences and expectations are.

findings.antecedent: Mood (worker happiness, well-being, job satisfaction)
findings.quote: The understanding of how mood influences productivity is weak. Different studies have emphasized worker happiness, well-being, and job satisfaction as predictors of productivity while others have suggested that productivity is itself a generator of feelings of happiness, well-being, and job satisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to daylight
findings.quote: Exposure to daylight can have both positive and negative effects on health.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to daylight outdoors (UV-B radiation)
findings.quote: The strongest effects occur outdoors. Exposure to daylight outdoors can cause tissue damage, which is bad, and generate vitamin D, which is good.

findings.antecedent: Daylight and sunlight delivered through glass (reduced UV-B, view out)
findings.consequent: UV-B radiation, stress, incidence of health problems (from electric lighting fluctuations)
findings.quote: Daylight and sunlight delivered through glass will have much less short wavelength ultra-violet (UV-B) radiation than the same radiation outdoors, but can still have adverse effects on people who are sensitive to ultra-violet radiation. ... Windows that provide a view out as well as daylight, can reduce stress and hence reduce the demand for health services. Daylight reduces the incidence of health problems caused by the rapid fluctuations in light output typical of electric lighting.

findings.antecedent: Wall containing windows
findings.consequent: Construction/maintenance costs, building operating costs, rental value
findings.quote: A wall containing windows costs more to construct and maintain than one without. These costs may be offset by reductions in building operating costs. However, the presence of windows is believed to have a positive effect on the rental value of a space.

findings.antecedent: Daylighting of a conventionally windowless retail space
findings.quote: Daylighting of a conventionally windowless retail space can have a positive effect on sales.

findings.antecedent: Windows with view of natural landscape (for prisoners/patients)
findings.consequent: Sick calls, hospital stay duration, negative comments from nurses
findings.quote: Moore (1981) studied the healthcare demands of prisoners, and found that those whose windows looked out over hills and farmland made significantly fewer sick calls to the prison infirmary than those whose windows overlooked the prison yard. View through a window has also been found to influence recovery from surgery. Ulrich (1984) found that patients whose rooms afforded a view of the natural landscape rather than of other buildings spent fewer days in hospital (7.96 compared with 8.70), and that nurses recorded fewer negative comments regarding their progress.

findings.antecedent: Windowless intensive care units
findings.quote: Similarly, Keep and Inman (1980) found that patients in a windowless intensive care units showed more confusion.

findings.antecedent: Daylight vs. electric lighting as primary source
findings.quote: There is no doubt that people prefer daylight over electric lighting as their primary source of illumination.

findings.antecedent: Windows (view out vs. admission of daylight)
findings.quote: The results of surveys of office workers suggest that of this list, the two most important attributes of windows are the view out and the admission of daylight (Collins, 1975; Brill, 1985). The importance of a view out is demonstrated by the work of Young and Berry (1979). They examined people's preference for an office with either a real window, providing both a view out and daylight in the office, or an artificial window showing a dynamic view of nature but providing very little light into the office. There was very little difference in the preferences for the two window types, implying that it is the view that is dominating the preference.

findings.antecedent: Small windowless offices (little opportunity to leave, lack of stimulation)
findings.consequent: Job satisfaction, satisfaction with physical environment, use of visual decor
findings.quote: Surveys of the occupants of windowless offices have shown that when the space is small and the occupant has little opportunity to leave the space, the occupants are less satisfied with their jobs and with the physical environment (Finnegan and Solomon (1981); and the lack of variety is noticeable and the lack of windows is disliked (Ruys, 1970). ... Some support for this view comes from the work of Heerwagen and Orians (1986). They observed that people occupying small private offices without windows used twice the number of visual materials to decorate their offices as did people whose offices had windows.

findings.antecedent: Direct sunlight, solar glare, radiant heating, passers-by (ground floors)
findings.quote: Measurements of the use of window blinds in multi-story office buildings have shown two trends. The first is that window blinds are most likely to be closed on ground floors where there are many passers-by, and, on all floors, as the sun begins to shine on the window and so cause solar glare and radiant heating (Maniccia et al., 1999). This might be expected. Less expected is the second trend, that many of these blinds are kept closed even after the sun has ceased to shine directly on the window; and that, in some cases, the blinds are left closed for days, months, or years (Rea, 1984).

findings.antecedent: Increased daylight in office
findings.quote: prolonged measurements in a set of deep, private offices with large windows have shown that, given the opportunity, people tend to increase the amount of electric light as the amount of daylight in the office increases (Begemann et al., 1994, 1995).

findings.antecedent: Carefully designed daylight delivered through windows
findings.consequent: Good lighting, environmental stimulation (variation, view out)
findings.quote: one reason why daylight is so popular as a means of lighting is that, if carefully designed, daylight delivered through windows provides a comprehensive package which can meet the requirements of good lighting by revealing both the task and the space clearly and the requirement of environmental stimulation by variation of lighting conditions in the space and a view out through the window.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to daylight (high illuminance at eye, matched spectrum)
findings.quote: exposure to daylight is a very potent means of providing enough light to entrain the circadian system. This is evident in a study by Eastman et al. (1994)... Further, the spectrum of daylight is better matched to the spectral sensitivity of the human circadian system, which shows a peak sensitivity at about 465 nm (Brainard et al., 2001; Thapan et al., 2001), than commonly used electric light sources...

findings.antecedent: Exposure to bright light (daylight) at appropriate times
findings.consequent: Advanced/delayed sleep phase disorder, sleep onset/maintenance insomnia
findings.quote: Exposure to light has been shown to be an effective treatment for these sleep disorders... What is clear is that daylight, assuming it is available at the required time, is a convenient means to provide the high light levels apparently required to sustain the operation of the circadian system.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to bright light (daylight)
findings.quote: What is clear is that exposure to bright light is often an effective treatment (Rosenthal et al., 1985; Terman et al., 1989; Tam et al., 1995)... there is no doubt that daylight could also be used as a source of 'bright light.'

findings.antecedent: Daylighting provided without glare (high light levels, good color rendering)
findings.consequent: Vision of Alzheimer's patients (reduced contrast sensitivity)
findings.quote: This finding, suggesting as it does that Alzheimer's patients are struggling to make sense of the world with diminished visual and cognitive capabilities, raises the intriguing possibility that daylighting, with its high light levels and good color rendering properties, would be of advantage for the visual capabilities of Alzheimer's patients, provided it is delivered without glare.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to bright light (daylight) during the day and little light at night
findings.consequent: Regularity of circadian rhythm, nighttime wandering, agitation in Alzheimer's patients
findings.quote: Exposure to bright light during the day has been shown to improve the regularity of their circadian rhythm, which will reduce the prevalence of such undesirable behavior as nighttime wandering... The result was reduced agitation and wandering at night and more stable rest / activity rhythms... Further, it may be that daylighting is the most convenient means of providing high light levels for people with Alzheimer's disease.

findings.antecedent: View of a natural scene through a window (real or simulated)
findings.quote: a view of a natural scene through a window (real or simulated) has been suggested as a means of relieving stress (Clearwater and Coss, 1991; Kaplan, 1992; Ulrich, 1993).

findings.antecedent: Prolonged exposure to the sun (radiation)
findings.quote: What is proven is that prolonged exposure to the sun results in skin aging.

findings.antecedent: Poor lighting (inadequate illuminance, excessive luminance ratios, lamp flicker) or poorly delivered daylight (excessive luminance ratios)
findings.quote: The symptoms of eyestrain, such as sore eyes, blurred vision, and headaches, can be produced by both electric lighting and daylighting.

findings.antecedent: High illuminances from daylighting, large-area/repetitive/high-contrast patterns
findings.consequent: Migraine attacks, visual discomfort in migraineurs
findings.quote: However, high illuminances such as are produced by daylighting will also tend to exacerbate the disturbing effects of any large-area, repetitive, high-contrast patterns.

findings.antecedent: High light levels and variation from daylighting (environmental stimulation)
findings.consequent: Arousal level, repetitive behavior in autistic children
findings.quote: The high light levels often provided by daylight are inherently arousing. Further, the variation in lighting of an interior that is associated with daylighting, especially when there are scattered clouds in the sky, can be regarded as a form of environmental stimulation.

findings.antecedent: Level of individual control of environment (lighting, heating, cooling, ventilation, noise)
findings.quote: For personal control, Leaman and Bordass (2000) report that there was a small but statistically significant correlation (r = 0.16 to 0.49) between level of individual control of the environment and self-reported productivity in seven of eleven office buildings evaluated in 1996-97. However, they also make the point that of the five different aspects of the physical environment examined; heating, cooling, lighting, ventilation, and noise, lighting control is the only one that is not statistically significantly linked to self-rated productivity.

findings.antecedent: Deeper buildings (requiring electric lighting/mechanical ventilation)
findings.quote: As for building depth, Leaman and Bordass (2000) report that as buildings get deeper, the levels of satisfaction with the building and self-reported productivity decrease. The critical threshold depth appears to be about 15 m, from wall to wall.

findings.antecedent: Best daylighting in classrooms
findings.consequent: Improvement in standardized test scores (reading, mathematics)
findings.quote: children in the classrooms with the best daylighting achieved a 20 to 26 percent greater improvement over the year than average.

findings.antecedent: Skylight design allowing patches of sunlight (visual/thermal discomfort)
findings.quote: Although most of their analyses show an improvement in test scores with more daylight, there is one analysis for skylights that shows a reduced improvement in test scores with greater daylight. This deterioration is explained by saying that the skylight design allowed patches of sunlight to strike the walls and students desks, with consequent potential for visual and thermal discomfort.

findings.antecedent: Daylight provided through windows or skylight (higher illuminance, matched spectrum)
findings.consequent: Production and timing of hormones (cortisol), ability to concentrate, sociability in children
findings.quote: What was found was a statistically significant interaction between the concentration of cortisol and classrooms... Further, the cortisol concentration was related to observations of the children's ability to concentrate and sociability, ability to concentrate being greater at low cortisol concentrations and sociability being greater under higher cortisol concentrations.
